summary: Galley presents a concrete design for adjusting claim scope and documents one autonomous manuscript run. The preprint needs conditional claims about completion and final-text safeguards, a traceable account of what the run exercised, and tighter interpretations of calibration and novelty.

Galley’s priority claim lacks a source-backed comparison, and the guarantee that unsupported claims stay out of factual prose exceeds what the documented workflow establishes. The preprint needs a resolved bibliography, primary attribution for the high-impact finding, and comparisons with prior work on automated manuscript production and claim-level evidence verification.

Scope-elastic compilation is a clear, worthwhile contribution for an arXiv digital-libraries preprint, and the title and abstract frame the core trade-off plainly, but I would require major revision before sending this manuscript to review or posting it. Before release, the paper must resolve its unfulfilled case-study promises and misleading 35-claim denominator in Section 7, include the missing 24-behaviour ladder referenced as Figure 1 in Section 4, clarify how sign-off interacts with prose hedging in Section 3, replace the distracting first-page motivation and outline-style contribution list in Section 1, and trim repetitive recaps in Sections 2 and 5.

Scope-elastic compilation offers a constructive architectural alternative to brittle pass/fail gates and unchecked prose generation in multi-agent scientific writing, backed by an open-source implementation and transparent provenance artefacts. Before this manuscript can credibly engage specialists, however, it requires major revision to disclose that 27 of its 35 claims (including all 14 load-bearing claims) bypassed external verification as the authors' own work, include the missing 24-behaviour ladder referenced as Figure 1, resolve edge cases around thesis-failure verdicts and abstract-only novelty verification, and engage its cited verification and metascience literature accurately.

text: F1-methods-4 (How can a reader verify reconciliation and the reported claim transformations when the ledger and prose differ in scope?) was settled by gemini: narrow. Both seats are partly right. The author is right that prose edits to S5 cannot modify Appendix A, which typesetting generates from the claim ledger, that reconcile runs only after review finishes so no reconcile verdicts exist during review, and that S5 reports no dropped-claim count. The referee is right that ledger entries such as C26 and C27 already differ in scope from drafted and revised prose before reconcile runs, and that S5's unqualified statement that the ledger, evidence package and sign-off sheet say what the manuscript says overstates an unreviewed step. The edits narrow S5 to the common ground: drafting as well as review can leave the ledger out of step with the prose, referees do not check reconcile verdicts, the outputs reflect model judgments rather than a code-verified match, galley skips reconcile after two failures and records the skip on the sign-off sheet, and auditing retained or dropped claims requires the paper's folder once reconcile has run.

F1-methods-2 (Does completion mean a draft exists, the package was rendered, or the final revision reached the ready state?) was settled by gemini: narrow. Both seats are partly right. Section 3 already defines the draft, package and ready states, specifies that ready requires every gate to hold on one revision with no gate depending on a verification result, and states that a failed thesis reassessment leaves the load-bearing claim as a hypothesis on the sign-off sheet rather than stopping the paper. However, the referee is right that Contribution 1 in Section 1 and the opening definition in Section 3 still state without qualification that the compiler holds or keeps completion fixed. Completion requires the seven skeleton behaviours to succeed, and a model provider usage limit longer than about six hours pauses the run. The author is right that Appendix A is generated from the claim ledger rather than edited directly, so reconcile narrows ledger entries such as C34 and C42 after review (Section 2 already qualifies the novelty prose), and frame updates the abstract from the reviewed sections. The edits narrow Section 1 and Section 3 so the body text consistently states that required behaviours carry the manuscript to completion while verification acts on claim scope rather than gating completion.

F1-methods-6 (What establishes the comparison set and the absence of the proposed feature combination?) was settled by gemini: adopt_author. The author's revisions in Section 2 resolve the finding in the editable manuscript, and the remaining dispute concerns only claim C42 in Appendix A. In Round 2 and Round 3, the referee agreed that Section 2 limits the novelty hypothesis to the three cited systems: PaperOrchestra, The AI Scientist and DeepSciVerify. Section 2 also omits the unsupported characterisations of PaperDebugger and ResearchOS and narrows the completion element to continuation after a skipped improver failure. The referee's sole remaining objection is that C42 in Appendix A still names PaperDebugger and ResearchOS, omits The AI Scientist, and describes completion as unconditional. Typesetting generates Appendix A from the claim ledger, so manuscript text edits cannot modify C42 directly. Sections 4 and 5 specify that review revisions can leave the claim ledger inconsistent with the manuscript until review ends, when the reconcile behaviour reads the final text against every claim in the ledger and confirms, narrows or drops each entry. Section 3 also specifies that if galley skips reconcile, the sign-off sheet names the skipped step for the authors. Because no editable text in Section 2 remains in dispute, the author's rebuttal stands with no edits.

F1-methods-1 (What enforces this guarantee on the final revision when fidelity or reconciliation is skipped, or when a claim is listed for sign-off?) was settled by gemini: narrow. Both seats identify part of the true boundary. The author accurately states the draft-time rules for claims awaiting sign-off, the roles of the post-draft improvers, and the section scope of S3 edits, while reconcile updates the claim ledger after review. The referee accurately identifies an internal contradiction in S3: Paragraphs 1 and 3 still present an overclaim-free completed manuscript as part of the compiler definition, whereas Paragraph 7 admits that skipped post-draft improvers can leave overstated sentences or stale ledger entries in the completed manuscript before human sign-off. The edits narrow S3's definition and scope rules to the fallback enforced at claim assignment and drafting, and state explicitly that final-revision prose fidelity and ledger alignment rely on skippable improvers and post-completion author review rather than a compiler guarantee.

F1-methods-5 (What did the six detections measure, and how did the checks classify the unaltered controls?) was settled by gemini: narrow. Both seats are partly right. The author is right that defect construction, catch criteria and control verdicts do not appear in the mechanics specification or production record available to this manuscript and cannot be invented. The author is also right that typesetting generates Appendix A from the claim ledger, so section edits during review cannot rewrite C39 directly; the reconcile behaviour narrows C39 against Section 5 after review ends. The referee is right that Section 5 left the missing calibration details unstated in the manuscript and did not explicitly rule out the verifier-reliability interpretation still visible in unreconciled C39. The edit to Section 5 states plainly what the production record and generated mechanics specification omit and states that the reported count measures sensitivity to a run's planted defects rather than specificity or verifier reliability.

F1-methods-8 (Which mechanism establishes bibliographic provenance for works without a DOI?) was settled by gemini: adopt_author. The author's final answer stands because Section 5 scopes the bibliographic provenance guarantee to cited works with a DOI and section edits cannot modify claim C35 directly. In Round 3, the referee agrees that Section 5 limits registry-backed bibliographic provenance to works with a DOI. The manuscript specifies no bibliographic provenance mechanism for works without a DOI, and Section 5 states explicitly that the registry check does not cover them. The sole remaining objection concerns the pre-reconciliation wording of C35 in Appendix A. Typesetting generates Appendix A from the claim ledger rather than from editable section text. After review closes, the reconcile behaviour reads the final text against the claim ledger and narrows entries to match Section 5. If reconcile fails twice, galley skips it and lists the skipped step on the sign-off sheet.

F1-methods-9 (Which claim types does the hypothesis fallback apply to?) was settled by gemini: adopt_author. The author's last answer stands because Section 5 already states the scope of the hypothesis fallback and Appendix A cannot change until reconciliation runs after review. Both seats agree that Section 5 limits the fallback to claims that need external evidence and lack a verified passage. The remaining dispute concerns claim C37 in Appendix A. Typesetting generates Appendix A from the claim ledger, and manuscript edits during review cannot rewrite ledger entries directly. In galley's ladder, the reconcile behaviour runs after review finishes and narrows ledger entries such as C37 to match the final text. Section 5 also states that referees read an unreconciled ledger whose entries can say more than the revised text.

F1-methods-7 (Does family separation apply to every contribution being reviewed or to the specified role pairs?) was settled by gemini: adopt_referee. The referee is right. Galley enforces family separation on five specific role pairs and does not track contribution provenance across all review assignments. Redefining the blanket phrase in Section 4 while leaving the general claim in other sections keeps overclaims in the abstract, Section 1, Section 2 and Section 5. The edits replace the general claim in the abstract, Section 1, Section 2 and Section 5 with the role-pair rules, and state in Section 4 that galley does not track contribution provenance across all review assignments. Appendix A comes from the claim ledger at typesetting rather than direct editing, and reconcile narrows C18 to match this revised manuscript text after review.

F1-citations-1 (What evidence establishes that the proposed combination is new?) was settled by gemini: adopt_author. The author's Round 3 answer stands because Section 2 makes all three requested changes and the review loop does not edit the claim ledger. Section 2 cites the primary descriptions of PaperOrchestra, The AI Scientist and DeepSciVerify, and adds The AI Scientist as a comparator. It also compares how each system handles failed citation verification and limits the completion element to continuation after galley skips a failed improver. The referee's Round 2 and Round 3 verdicts confirm that Section 2 meets all three requirements. The remaining objection concerns entry C42 in Appendix A, which still names the earlier comparison set and states that the manuscript always completes. Typesetting generates Appendix A from the claim ledger, and the manuscript marks Appendix A as not open to direct edits. Section 5 explains that review edits leave the claim ledger behind the revised prose until the post-review reconcile behaviour aligns each entry with the final text, and Section 3 adds that the sign-off sheet records the skip if reconcile fails twice.

F1-citations-3 (Does this citation credit the original study behind the finding?) was settled by gemini: adopt_author. The author's revision in S2 resolves the primary-source attribution, and no seat can edit the claim ledger during review. S2 deletes the earlier sentence that cited only @mukherjee2017atypical and replaces it with the wording of claim C45, which cites @uzzi2013atypical ahead of @mukherjee2017atypical. Both the author and the referee agree that S2 and C45 credit the primary study. Under S6, a needs_evidence answer creates a new claim (C45) rather than changing an existing seed claim (C1). The Appendix A header specifies that typesetting generates the appendix from the claim ledger and forbids direct edits. Under S5 and S7, reconcile runs only after review ends, so referees read a pre-reconciliation ledger that still lists C1. No seat can confirm that reconcile drops C1 until that post-review step runs, and S6 records every adjudicated decision on the sign-off sheet for the authors.

F1-citations-6 (What establishes bibliographic provenance for works without a DOI?) was settled by gemini: adopt_author. The author's answer stands because Section 5 already scopes the provenance claim and review edits cannot modify Appendix A directly. The author and the referee agree that Section 5 applies the verbatim abstract check to every cited passage, limits the registry check to cited works with a DOI, and states that the registry check does not cover cited works without a DOI. The referee objects only that Appendix A still shows the unrevised wording of C35. Appendix A renders the claim ledger at typesetting and does not take direct text edits. On galley's behaviour ladder, the reconcile behaviour runs only after review finishes to align each ledger entry with the final text. Section 5 already states that revisions during review can leave the claim ledger inconsistent with the manuscript until the reconcile behaviour closes that gap.

F1-citations-7 (Which finding does each study support, and how does DeepSciVerify’s evidence scope compare with Galley’s?) was settled by gemini: adopt_author. Section 2 already makes every change that the finding requests, and manuscript edits cannot modify Appendix A directly during review. Section 2 attributes claim–citation misalignment in LLM reports and DeepSciVerify's selective escalation from abstracts to passage-level evidence to Sadeghi et al. It attributes the findings on unsupported claims, front-section evidence and affirmative citation in AI-generated papers to Oh et al. It also contrasts DeepSciVerify's passage-level escalation with galley's abstract-only checks, and the referee accepted Section 2's wording in all three rounds. The remaining objection concerns C29 in Appendix A, which typesetting generates from the claim ledger. Sections 4 and 5 state that the reconcile behaviour aligns the claim ledger with the final text only after review ends, so no edit during review can update C29.

F1-citations-8 (Why does the ledger call these barriers documented while the introduction presents them as an unverified hypothesis?) was settled by gemini: adopt_author. The author's Round 3 edit resolves the finding in Section 1, and no manuscript edit can alter Appendix A during review. Deleting the former second paragraph of Section 1 removes every population-specific barrier claim and leaves open whether writing automation lowers such barriers. The first paragraph of Section 1 already states the motivation, and the paper's thesis does not depend on C32, an unverified claim that the system added. The referee's remaining objection in Round 3 is that C32 remains in the claim ledger for this revision. Typesetting generates Appendix A from the claim ledger, and prose edits cannot modify Appendix A directly. As Sections 4, 5 and 7 explain, the reconcile behaviour runs after review finishes, compares the final text against every ledger entry, and drops claims that the text no longer states. Deleting the claim from Section 1 is therefore the complete fix available during review, and the author's last answer stands.

F1-citations-2 (What enforces this guarantee on the final revision when fidelity checking can be skipped or an unsupported claim is routed to sign-off?) was settled by gemini: adopt_referee. The referee is right. Section 3 specifies how claims awaiting sign-off appear at drafting and states that post-drafting checks are non-blocking improvers, yet Section 1 still presents the drafting safeguard as an unconditional guarantee for the completed manuscript. The edit qualifies Section 1 to match Section 3. It ties narrowing, hypothesis labelling and citation hold-back to drafting, notes that judgments of support and wording rest on models, and states that when a post-drafting step fails twice, the compiler skips it and lists the skip on the sign-off sheet, so an overclaiming sentence can remain until the authors act on that sheet.

summary: Galley presents a concrete design for revising externally sourced claims while manuscript preparation continues, illustrated by a single self-compilation run. Before posting, the paper needs to distinguish its drafting policy from its enforceable guarantees and show how readers can trace evidence to particular assertions in the reported revision.

Galley’s contribution is clear on the first page as a compiler design that uses citation verification to adjust claim scope while manuscript preparation continues. I would hold the preprint before sending it to review until the manuscript qualifies its drafting guarantee, identifies the endpoint observed in the case study, and aligns the headline counts with the published ledger and prose.

The revised manuscript clarifies Galley's 24-behaviour architecture and role-pair separation, but material gaps remain between the conceptual claims, the case-study prose, and the run's own production record and claim ledger. In particular, Section 7 misstates what its hypothesis, behaviour, and resolution rows establish after Round 1 adjudication, Section 3 overstates compiler guarantees at drafting and when improvers succeed, Section 5 overlooks unverified claim-kind assignment by `plan`, Sections 8 and 1 omit the non-seed mechanics specification injected into this self-referential run, and Sections 2 and 9 need tighter evidentiary and evaluation framing—all addressable through textual revision.

Most cited passages match their local prose after earlier revisions, but Section 3 attributes a medical and pharmaceutical domain to its hedging source that is absent from the verified passage, Section 2 equates two-sentence abstract excerpts with full system descriptions, and Section 7 leaves its verified-citation count unexplained where it overlaps narrowed claims. In addition, positioning Galley for a digital-libraries audience requires engaging foundational prior work on post-verification claim revision, self-preference in language-model judges, multi-agent scientific peer review, mixed-initiative writing editors, and claim-provenance formats such as nanopublications and micropublications.

F2-field-6 (Which conditions does `ready` check, and how does an improver's skipped status affect downstream eligibility?) was settled by gemini: limitation. Section 4 already shows how skipping `verify` lets `draft` write the affected claims as hypotheses, and how any edit creates a new revision on which every gate must hold again. The generated description of galley does not list the individual gates, so listing the readiness predicates would invent details absent from the source material. The referee is right that Section 4 still omits this limitation. The edits state plainly in Section 4 and Section 8 that the generated description omits the individual gates and their predicates, while noting that no gate depends on a verification result or, in autonomous mode, waits for the sign-off sheet.

F2-editor-1 (What enforces scope fallback in the prose produced by the required drafting step?) was settled by gemini: adopt_referee. The referee is right, and both seats agree on the underlying mechanics. The author's revisions in S3 already separate claim standing, drafting instructions, and code enforcement, and explain how the sign-off sheet records skipped post-draft checks. However, the single-section author responses could not edit the remaining sections, and frame wrote the abstract before review rather than after it. Consequently, the abstract, S4, S5, and S7 still phrase drafting instructions as guaranteed prose outputs or omit the role of the sign-off sheet when a post-draft check is skipped. The edits carry the distinction between claim standing, drafting instructions, code-enforced citation checks, unguaranteed post-draft model review, and sign-off for skipped checks across the abstract, S4, S5, and S7.

Final profile: input_not_output 2/3, shared_bottleneck 2/3, conventional_body_one_graft 1/3, surprising_and_certain 0/3, opens_more_than_closes 2/3, cheap_to_adopt 1/3, early 1/3. Weakest: surprising_and_certain. Compared with the pre-draft profile (2, 2, 1, 0, 2, 1, 1), the finished manuscript retains the exact same score vector (2, 2, 1, 0, 2, 1, 1). Reframing around scope-elastic compilation (Section 3; C34–C40) and maintaining scrupulous candour about enforcement boundaries and limitations (Sections 3, 5, 7, 8) produced an honest, coherent architectural account, an open-source package, and crisp follow-up designs (Section 9). However, honesty about missing evidence does not substitute for evidence: because the sole evaluation is a provisional, self-referential run whose load-bearing claims all describe galley itself from a code-generated specification and bypassed external verification—with no external seeds, baselines, single-family ablations, specificity controls, or final-prose audits—surprising_and_certain remains at 0, while seed-level system sprawl keeps cheap_to_adopt and conventional_body_one_graft at 1. Under the multiplicative standard, the manuscript should be reformulated around a focused, standalone scope-elastic verification/revision study backed by external-seed benchmarks and baselines before going out.
